crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Syndromic Surveillance
children.blurb: Syndromic surveillance uses pre-diagnostic health data, such as emergency department chief complaints, over-the-counter medication sales, school absenteeism, and calls to nurse advice lines, to detect unusual patterns that may signal an outbreak or public health threat.

children.name: Outbreak Mapping
children.blurb: Outbreak mapping uses AI to detect, visualize, and forecast disease spread across populations.

children.name: Vaccine Waning Models
children.blurb: Vaccine waning models estimate how protection from vaccination declines over time, using observed infection, hospitalization, or antibody data.

children.name: Social Determinants of Health
children.blurb: Social determinants of health (SDOH) refer to the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age, including housing, income, education, employment, food access, transportation, and social support.

children.name: Allocating Scarce Resources
children.blurb: Allocating scarce resources in epidemiology and population health covers the use of AI to decide who gets a limited good or service when demand exceeds supply.

sections.body: This field applies machine learning to population level health questions rather than individual diagnosis. AI is currently used to scan emergency department records, pharmacy sales, and search queries for early signs of disease clusters, a practice called syndromic surveillance. Outbreak mapping systems combine case reports with mobility data to show where an infection is spreading in near real time. Vaccine waning models estimate how protection from a dose declines across a population using observational data. Work on social determinants of health uses routine data like housing, income, and food access to predict which groups face higher risk, and scarce resource allocation models help hospitals or public health agencies rank who gets limited supplies during a crisis.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Syndromic surveillance can flag known diseases like influenza or COVID-19 with reasonable accuracy, but it often produces false alarms from noise in data. Outbreak mapping is most reliable for diseases with clear case definitions and reporting, and much weaker for novel pathogens or places with sparse testing. Vaccine waning models are limited by confounding, because people who get vaccinated early often differ from those who get vaccinated late. Social determinants models can describe disparities but have not consistently shown they improve outcomes when used to direct services. Scarce resource allocation remains ethically contested and technically hard to validate, since real crises are rare and simulations cannot capture all human factors. Across the 1000 medical AI models tracked on this site, epidemiology tools are a minority, and most have not been tested in live public health emergencies.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The five pages move from detecting a threat to responding to it. Syndromic Surveillance explains how AI watches for early signals in messy, everyday data, and a reader would start there to understand detection. Outbreak Mapping then shows how those signals become geographic pictures of spread, useful for seeing where an outbreak is moving. Vaccine Waning Models shifts from infection to immunity, covering how long protection lasts in a population and why booster timing is hard to predict. Social Determinants of Health steps back to the underlying conditions that shape who gets sick, and it connects the earlier pages to questions of fairness. Allocating Scarce Resources is the final, hardest step, where models try to turn all this information into decisions about who receives limited care or supplies.
